item.title: Was the Bible really produced without errors?
item.description: Inerrancy as an almost meaningless claim
item.content:encoded:
Biblical inerrancy is the concept that the Bible is without errors of any kind in the original manuscripts. This is an essential doctrine in American evangelicalism.

As stated by The Gospel Coalition "The doctrine of the authority and inerrancy of Scripture is that, as a corollary of the inspiration of Scripture, the God-breathed Scriptures are wholly true in all things that they assert in the original autographs and therefore function with the authority of God’s own words."

In other words, when the 66 ancient books of the Bible, from Genesis to Revelation, were written down by humans over a span of (purportedly) 1600 years, God guided the process so that every word in every document was without error in the original "autographs", that is, the pages actually written by Isaiah, Paul, etc.

This was once my belief. I now see it to be, well, not even wrong, but meaningless - that is, it cannot be tested and it doesn't really tell us anything about the Bibles we have now. Instead, the belief in inerrancy serves as an article of faith, a boundary marker for identifying who is "faithful" to Scripture and who is not.

But here are some of the problems with it.

Inerrancy applies only to the original manuscripts (the 'autographs'). We are SO far from having the original manuscripts of any document in the Bible. In fact, with books like Genesis or the Gospels which show signs of being compiled from earlier stories, lists of sayings, and even orally-passed traditions, it is difficult to define what the "original manuscript" is.

The most recent manuscripts of New Testament documents are fragments, copies that were made starting in the early second century, with a few tiny fragments possibly from late in the first century. These, along with the many later copies, bear all the marks of human-copied material: Spelling errors, repeated lines, content inserted in the margin because the scribe maybe forgot it the first time. One of the things that makes the ancient Bible manuscripts so fascinating is to compare the ways they are different, and to note the things that seem to get added in or dropped as time passes.

One well known example of this is the famous story from John's gospel about Jesus and the adulterous women ("Let he who is without sin cast the first stone"). Nearly every modern English translation of John, even ones favored by evangelicals, acknowledges that this short story does not appear in the oldest sources, and that in some manuscripts it appears elsewhere in John, or even in Luke's gospel.

Whenever you see a footnote in your Bible that says "Some ancient sources say...", the translators are telling you that when you compare the ancient manuscripts, there is an alternate version of the text that appears in enough copies to mention. And in a Bible that contains such footnotes, you see them on practically every page.

Does this mean the Bible is riddled with errors? I don't think so. In comparison with other ancient works, the text of the Bible is very well-established. The vast majority of those footnotes I mentioned deal with small and fairly insignificant differences.

But to say that the original writings were without error tells us nothing about the Bible as we actually have it. Further, there is no evidence for this claim. It is asserted because belief in an inerrant Bible is a useful tool for telling people how to live and for accumulating power over others.

Most of us read the Bible in a language other than ancient Hebrew and Greek. If we DID have the original writings (we don't) and the experts could tell us with certainty, "Yes, these are without error" (a fantasy), that would be significant. But I couldn't read them. I need an English translation. And I'm in luck. There are dozens of them, many of them produced or updated in the 21st century.

Why are there dozens of them? Well, each one was produced because someone thought that the others didn't get it quite right.

When I was a kid, I thought that learning Spanish would involve nothing more than taking a sentence in American English and swapping out the words with Spanish ones. I later found out that the two languages have different ideas about sentence structure, the use of gender, verb tenses, pronunciation, etc., making it impossible to precisely translate a Spanish book to English. Compromises have to be made, and different translators make different choices about how to convey the original meaning in the receptor language. And Spanish and English are fairly closely-related.

Imagine the greater difficulty in translating an ancient language into modern English (which, by the way, is itself always changing). There is simply no perfect way to do it. Each English translation makes dozens of choices. How "literal" should we try to be? How much freedom do we have to rearrange an ancient sentence into something modern readers can understand? When the text says something about "all men" and we know it means "all people", can we say it that way or not?

Every translation team also makes choices that reflect a theological perspective - their own or that of their intended readers. The New International Version, for example, often smoothes out textual difficulties in a way that fits with the expectations of evangelical readers. The NRSV, the favorite Bible of mainline churches (and almost never seen among evangelicals) uses inclusive language almost to the point of distraction. And as you might imagine, these two Bibles differ in how they render verses that deal with same-sex relationships.

The point is that there is no one way to translate from Greek and Hebrew to English, so no two English translations are the same. And we've hardly mentioned the difficulty of translating from an ancient and very foreign culture to a modern one. This is, of course, all very obvious and normal. It's just that a theory about original manuscripts without errors has nothing to do with the Bibles we have.

Just because we all read the same words doesn't mean we all read the same thing. Even if we all read the same Bible (which we don't because of the above), we have a way of seeing different things in it. My father-in-law used to say that "we don't see things as they are, we see things as WE are". Nowhere is this more evident than in the number of Christian denominations across the world.

By some estimates, there are more than 45,000 Christian denominations, though this is a bit misleading because many churches from the same tradition are divided by country, language, etc. into official denominations. In the United States there are several hundred denominations. Each of the major branches of Christianity (Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, etc.) was established (in part) because people disagreed about what God's plan was for ordering church and society.

Beginning with the Protestant Reformation around the 1500s, the Bible took center stage as the revelation of God's plan for our lives (not coincidentally because the printing press was invented at about the same time, so text-based authority became possible). From the start, Protestantism has been characterized by dividing, and sometime by ugly skirmishes and even wars, over differences in interpretation (Luther and Calvin, right out of the gate, came up with two very different ideas about Christianity based on their understanding of the Bible). Nearly all of those several hundred denominations in the U.S. are descendants of the Protestant Reformation.

When my parents started taking us to church, they chose a denomination where people believed that speaking in tongues and proclaiming prophetic messages were supposed to be part of worship, and every Sunday they did their best to prove it. After a few years, we started attending a church closer to home, where they believed that miraculous gifts like speaking in tongues and prophecy had definitely ceased when the last of Jesus' apostles died off, and that people today who did such things were either faking it or dabbling with demons. As a young adult, I took a middle position between the two, which made me a compromiser or a coward in the eyes of the stalwarts of my previous churches (though they were nice about it!)

The most important question in the Bible (according to many Protestants but by no means all) is: "What must I do to be 'saved'"? Being "saved" means (to many Protestants but by no means all) having your sins forgiven so you can go on living forever with God when you die. The Bible should provide a clear answer to that. And it does. In fact, it provides several.

I belonged to a religious group (we didn't like to be called a denomination) that took a minority view on this question. We found our clear answer in Acts 2:38 where it says to repent and be baptized for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit. Our adherence to this verse made other Christians think of us as strange legalists. It wasn't the command to "repent", to turn away from our sins. Most (but by no means all) Christians think that salvation should involve repentance on our part. It was the command to be baptized (and by "baptism", we meant being dunked completely under water) that caused others to consider us weird.

Why didn't they see it like we did? Acts 2:38 couldn't be clearer.

But other verses are equally clear with a different message. John 3:16 is the most famous of them, where "whosoever believeth in him shall not perish but inherit everlasting life". No mention of baptism or even repentance here.

Christian belief about salvation spans a wide spectrum and Christians disagree about even the very basics, like: Do you have to make a "decision for Christ" or can you gradually grow into belief? Are people free to accept or reject God, or are they predestined from the foundation of the world to do one or the other? Is repentance part of being saved or a result of it? Can you lose your salvation? Is it an individual matter, or can a father decide for his whole family?

Each of these positions can be defended with teaching or examples from the New Testament...as long as you ignore other teachings and examples from the New Testament. This is, in fact, what Christianity in America looks like today.

Even if the original documents of Scripture were communicated from God to people without errors, how is that relevant to the Bible that we have, in which Christians can find dozens or hundreds of issues about which there are disagreements important enough to divide over?

Inerrancy is a boundary-marker, a fence to separate "us" from "them". It is backed by no evidence and it says nothing meaningful about the Bibles that we have or the different ways we read them.

item.title: The Age of Reason
item.content:encoded:
Any seeker of reason would do well to read Thomas Paine's The Age of Reason, the classic popularization of deism which was first published in the United States at the beginning of the republic (1797-1807). In a brief and straightforward text, Paine lays out his case regarding the Bible (its inspiration, authority, and morality), supernatural revelation, the authority of religious organizations, etc.

Paine wasn't a biblical scholar. But his writing provides a layperson's overview of the content and history of the Bible that has long been understood by scholars but is still nearly unheard of by religious zealots who make policy today.

In a better world, students at seminaries and Bible colleges would study The Age of Reason alongside their survey courses of the Hebrew Bible and the New Testament. And Sunday School superintendents, members of local school boards, and Congress people would actually read the whole Bible (many never have) and Paine.

Key quote: (The religious person) despises the choicest gift of God to man, the gift of Reason; and having endeavoured to force upon himself the belief of a system against which reason revolts, he ungratefully calls it human reason, as if man could give reason to himself" (Part 1, ch. 8)

item.title: Sunday Truth
item.description: What we risk by believing impossible things
item.content:encoded:
During my ministry days, we used to ask potential Sunday School teachers to describe in writing their understanding of the Trinity. The variety of answers we received reminded me of something I heard in college: "If you ask your church members to explain the Trinity, you'll get ten or fifteen incompatible explanations, all of which have been declared heretical by the church."

But that was fine, because all we were looking for was something like: "I believe that there is only one God, and that he exists in three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit." If someone got that much, anything else was gravy.

The problem is: The statement above is a faith statement about the Trinity, but in no way is it an explanation. Rather, it lays out a seeming impossibility, and says: "I believe it." If I heard this for the first time, with no understanding of Christian doctrine, or if I heard a similar statement from someone from another religion, I'd have to ask: "What can that possibly mean? How is that not three gods?"

Nevertheless, the statement above was fine with us, and that's because the Trinity is something that I now think of as a Sunday Truth.

I got the term Sunday Truth from the 20th century philosopher Bertrand Russell. In one of his essays, Russell imagines that a government with enough power could get its people to believe any ridiculous thing, such as that water freezes when it gets hot and boils when it gets cold.

"Of course, even when these beliefs had been generated, people would not put the kettle in the ice-box when they wanted it to boil. That cold makes water boil would be a Sunday truth, sacred and mystical, to be professed in awed tones, but not to be acted on in daily life...any verbal denial of the mystic doctrine would be made illegal, and obstinate heretics would be 'frozen' at the stake. No person who did not enthusiastically accept the official doctrine would be allowed to teach or to have any position of power. Only the very highest officials, in their cups, would whisper to each other what rubbish it all is; then they would laugh and drink again." - Essays in Skepticism, pt. 2, Intellectual Rubbish

Even as a minister, I realized that we didn't expect anyone to be able to understand or explain the Trinity. The actual Christian doctrines of the Trinity were hammered out over the first four centuries of the church, in response to conflicting teachings about Jesus that had gained enough traction to be a problem. And the doctrines are complex, confusing, and hard to follow. Check out Wikipedia's entry on the Trinity and see how long you can keep reading. 😎

Not only that, but every explanation I learned in Sunday School as a child turned out to be heretical. One teacher told us, "Just as a woman can be a mom, a sister, a daughter, a wife, even though she is still one person..." Nope, that's modalism (which says that God is one being who relates to creation in three ways), condemned as a heresy in the 400s.

Another teacher said: "Your body has a heart and lungs and kidneys but it's one body..." Nope, that's partialism (which sees father, son and spirit are each part of God, but only fully God when combined), condemned as heresy in the 600s.

Mostly when people talk about the members of the trinity, they seem to slip into tritheism (which says there are three gods who work together, a divine Justice League). I once heard a preacher describe God (the father) thinking about whether to create the world, and then the preacher added: "Then God turned to Jesus and said, 'You know that if we do this thing, you're gonna have to go down there and die for their sins!"

Explanations like these are common because they actually make sense. The "orthodox" explanation (which, though based on various Bible passages, took centuries to hammer out) does not.

I recently rediscovered a favorite quote from Thomas Jefferson from an 1822 letter. He sets up the favorite quote by writing that "the Athanasian* paradox that one is three, and three but one, is so incomprehensible to the human mind, that no candid man can say he has any idea of it, and how can he believe what presents no idea? He who thinks he does, only deceives himself."

I think that few Christians would claim to understand the Trinity. Yet they swear that they believe it, adding that it's a "divine mystery", and that "God's thoughts are higher than ours." It's a Sunday Truth, after all.

I used to think that too, and I didn't see the harm. But that leads me to the quote I mentioned. Continuing on about the one who claims to understand the Trinity, Jefferson says:

"He proves, also, that man, once surrendering his reason, has no remaining guard against absurdities the most monstrous, and like a ship without a rudder, is the sport of every wind. With such persons gullibility which they call faith, takes the helm from the hand of reason, and the mind becomes a wreck."

Jefferson might have added something well-known in the early days of the Republic, and increasingly apparent today: When such persons take the helm of government, the nation becomes a wreck too.

*Refers to the Athanasian Creed which, 300 years after Jesus, defined the orthodox understanding of the Trinity.

item.title: Does Religion "Poison Everything?"
item.content:encoded:
One time I was walking through an empty hospital waiting room when on the television I saw a guy teaching passionately about Biblical prophecy. This wasn't a tele-evangelist or a mega-church "Brylcreem prophet" but a layman - thin, a beard, in a shirt-and-tie - maybe an engineer by day, or a teacher or an accountant. He was intelligent and he had elaborate (but not-professional) charts and graphs, and he poured his heart into teaching a tiny audience via public-access tv about his vision and calculations for the end times.

I was a minister at the time, but I had seen a lot of strife between Christians regarding differing views about prophecy, and I had also had too much of my own time wasted by ersatz prophecy experts. I also knew that 100% of end-times predictions have failed ("so far", I know). So I didn't feel good about what I saw. What I felt was:

"What a waste. So much intellectual effort and human passion, poured into this."

Then I wondered about the man on tv. "Maybe he works at IBM, or Denso or John Deere. He's probably been at his career for 15 years or more, and maybe he has a wife and three kids. He's good at his job, but it's nothing to live for. He longs for a bigger challenge, something with meaning commensurate with his desire to make a difference. And this is what hooked him."

Of course, none of that may be close to the truth. It's actually more a description of my own strivings for meaning and significance. And, as I increasingly realize, my Dad's. He really was an engineer and he had a nice, comfortable job as a professor of engineering. He had a wife and eventually five kids, and as his 30s rolled around, I think he was looking for something more significant. He and Mom bought a farm. He took a shot at starting a "tech company" (making printed circuit boards) in the 70s.

And (more to our point) he and Mom got us involved in a charismatic (speaking in tongues) evangelical church. And for awhile anyway, Dad got passionate about the Bible, investing himself in some unique and, um, unorthodox theories. If that pursuit had taken a major part of the rest of his life, well, what a waste that would have been. But it didn't.

When the famous atheist Christopher Hitchens wrote his 2007 book God Is Not Great, he gave it the subtitle: "How religion poisons everything". Hitchens was entertaining and funny and often bombastic, as you can see in his many YouTube videos. "Religion poisons EVERYTHING" is typical Hitchens - over the top and offensive to many. I can't quite agree. Then again, religion, as the great poet said, has "been the ruin of many a poor boy, and God, I know I'm one!"

Not really. I wasn't ruined by religion, and neither was Dad, and I hope that the guy on the hospital tv wasn't either. But boy, all three of us wasted some serious time and emotion trying to squeeze modern life and science and experience into an ancient frame. We (well, I, at least) let our compassion and generosity and humanness be limited by what our religion taught us about faithfulness and right thinking. Religion may not poison everything, but it poisons a lot.

Case-in-point: I recently checked in with one of my old mentors to see what he was writing and doing these days. Honestly, "mentor" is a strong word. I only met him once (although that "once" was a whole week spent with him, along with a very small group of other ministers). It was through his sermon tapes that I knew him and learned from him. He had a huge influence on me. And not only me. Once at a preacher's conference, the man who introduced my mentor said, "He doesn't know this, but he and I have been writing sermons together for a long time!" A lot of us were doing that. My mentor was often quoted, occasionally plagiarized, and always admired. He was interesting, funny, and he had a way of cutting to the heart of every matter. His was among the first mega-churches I ever knew about.

In 2016, my mentor was the first Christian leader I heard say (in an article) that he was going to "hold his nose and vote for Trump". His reasons were familiar to me, because I used to espouse them myself, and they were commonplace among evangelicals: "Families are under attack. Abortion is running rampant. Gay marriage has just been legalized. Trump may not be our ideal, but we aren't voting for a pastor, we're voting for a president." In 2016, I could still understand why he would say that. But I couldn't buy it myself anymore. After that, I found my way out of the ministry and lost contact with what he was writing.

So, just recently, I decided to look up my mentor again. He's now in his late 70s, I suppose, and retired but continues to write funny, insightful, winsome articles on a blog and on social media. I scanned through some of his writing and realized that he still has the gift.

Then I thought: "I wonder what he had to say about the last election." I didn't see many posts about it, but one right before the election said (my paraphrase):

"We all understand the need to vote our Christian values. One candidate favors unrestricted abortion. The other, while not perfect, appointed justices to the Supreme Court that overturned Roe v. Wade. Other important issues include the fact that religious liberty is in danger, as is the sanctity of marriage and the ability to protect our children from sinful sexual teachings. In the Bible, God uses imperfect people to do his will. Let's pray that God will use an imperfect president to slow the social and moral decline that has become so pervasive."

I wonder if he sees in the last 14 months a slowing of the social and moral decline in this country. I sure don't.

As wise and talented as this guy is, his idea of the most pressing and important issues facing our country has almost nothing to do with the teachings of Jesus, but instead consists of an amalgamation of right-wing political scare-topics cloaked in piety and religious authority. You might get the idea from his article that Jesus spent his time pleading with his followers to stand up for religious liberty, oppose abortion, and protect children from hearing that homosexuals exist.

Jesus of course never mentioned any of these things. He did have a few things to say about feeding the hungry, comforting the sick and dying, loving your enemies, and helping the starving beggar at the gate. None of that made it into my mentor's summary of our religious duty. Instead his "imperfect" president has unleashed a reign of terror against working immigrants and their families (these are the real "families under attack"), has cut spending on programs that, while "imperfect", keep people alive, while remodeling the White House and planning an expensive ballroom. I could go on.

Maybe religion really does poison everything. It made this good man (and many others, good and not-so-good) define morality not as compassion or helping people or living a good life but as enforcing a cruel conformity on people without understanding who they are or why they do what they do.

We needed more from guys like my mentor. We didn't get it.

item.title: Questions in Genesis
item.description: Two creation stories open the Bible and set us up for a world of sorrow and order.
item.content:encoded:
Many years into my former life as a pastor, and many years after I had earned two degrees from a Bible College, I read a simple statement that said that the Bible’s first book, Genesis, begins with TWO creation stories, one that happens in water and one that happens in a desert. I had never considered that before, but I realized immediately that the author was right.

Of course I was familiar with the stories the author was talking about. They are contained in the first three chapters of Genesis. But I had always considered this text as a single story, “The Creation Story”, one of the most important stories not only in the Bible but in the modern-day culture wars.

I had noticed significant differences between Genesis 1 and Genesis 2–3. As a minister, I had explained this by saying that Genesis 1 is the big picture of creation, and Genesis 2–3 zooms in to give more detail about the creation of humans and animals. But when I looked closer, I had to admit that I would never have seen them as a single unified story if they weren’t in the Bible and therefore (to my way of thinking at the time) exempt from scrutiny.

Let me highlight some of the differences.

Story One is contained in Genesis 1:1–2:3¹ and covers the well-known six-day creation account, with a day of rest for God on the seventh day. Story Two runs from Genesis 2:4 to the end of Genesis 3, and contains the equally well-known story of the Garden of Eden where God forms the woman from the man’s side. It tells of the serpent in the garden, the forbidden fruit, and the expulsion of the man and the woman from the garden. Both stories speak of the creation of animals, plants, and humans. But they deal with these matters in very different ways, using very different styles, for very different purposes.

And (significantly) each story uses a different name for God. Story One speaks of God with the word Elohim, which is not a proper name but a plural noun that denotes divine beings, much like the English word ‘god(s)’. Elohim is rendered ‘God’ in English Bibles.

Story Two calls God by the proper name Yahweh, which is rendered “LORD God” in most English Bibles. For context, when the Bible later forbids taking “the name of the LORD your God in vain” (Exodus 20:7), it is this name, Yahweh, that it mentions.²

Story One begins with Elohim and water:

In the beginning God (Elohim) created the heavens and the earth. And the earth was a formless and desolate emptiness, and darkness was over the surface of the deep, and the Spirit of God was hovering over the surface of the waters (Genesis 1:1–2, NASB³)

There is no hint of the much later theological idea of creation ex nihilo, from nothing. Instead, Elohim will pull order out of preexisting chaos. He will push aside the primeval waters which represent the frightening dark unknown, and will bring forth light, and life of every kind, and order in every way.

Story Two starts with Yahweh and a desert. This story begins shortly after the creation of the heavens and the earth. There is no water and no apparent life. But there is the dust of the ground, which will be Yahweh’s building material.

Story One describes creation as a six-day event, plus an additional seventh day on which Elohim rested. Story Two says explicitly that it is telling us about “the day” that Yahweh created the heavens and the earth: “This is the account of the heavens and the earth when they were created, in the day that the Lord God (Yahweh) made earth and heaven” (Genesis 2:4).

Story One is intensely orderly. In seven days, Elohim 1) called forth light and separated it from darkness, 2) created a livable space between the waters above and below (some have likened this new world to a snow-globe-like space, surrounded on all sides by water, 3) separated dry land from water and spoke into existence all manner of plant life, 4) created the sun, moon, and stars to move about on the roof of the dome which held back the waters above, and to mark out days and seasons and years, 5) created birds and sea animals, 6) created land animals and humans, and 7) took a day of rest, which isn’t technically part of creation, but is certainly part of the story of Elohim’s ordering of things. Elohim sanctified the seventh day as a special day.

In Story Two, Yahweh doesn’t work through a structured plan (as Elohim does in Story 1). He’s more experimental. Yahweh takes a step, then evaluates the results, then takes another step. He makes a man. He plants a garden, and puts the man there to cultivate it and tend to it.

Then Yahweh steps back (so to speak) and evaluates his work and says: “It is not good for the man to be alone; I will make him a helper suitable for him.”

At this point, it is fairly clear (unless your translation obscures it⁴) that Yahweh now creates the animals and birds and brings them before the man.

The man gives them names. But there is more going on here. This part of the story is intended to be understood as a search for a suitable companion for the man. Here’s the brief description in the NASB:

Then the Lord God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone; I will make him a helper suitable for him.” And out of the ground the Lord God formed every animal of the field and every bird of the sky, and brought them to the man to see what he would call them; and whatever the man called a living creature, that was its name. The man gave names to all the livestock, and to the birds of the sky, and to every animal of the field, but for Adam⁵ there was not found a helper suitable for him (Genesis 2:18–20).

Note how differently Story Two describes creation. In a barren world, Yahweh formed a man. Then he planted a garden and put the man there to care for it. Then, since the man had no companion, Yahweh began creating animals and brought them to the man, who named them all. But “for Adam, no suitable helper was found”.

If we allow Story One and Story Two to stand on their own, we can’t help but notice how Story Two differs from the six-day, orderly creation of Story One. And why not? They are making different points about God and humans.

But if it is necessary to harmonize the two stories — and it is necessary for many Christian evangelicals who take these stories as entries into a historical record — then the thing to do is to hammer and bend the texts so they sort of sound like they’re saying the same thing. The typical evangelical approach (which I used to apply) is the one I mentioned at the start — that Story Two gives us more details about the sixth day of Story One — even though the two accounts have very little in common.

So, back to Story Two. There is no suitable helper for the man, so Yahweh puts him to sleep and removes a rib from his side, and fashions a woman from it.

Now we are getting to the different objectives of each story. In both stories, humankind is portrayed as a special part of creation. In Story One, Elohim brings most of creation into existence with his command (“Let there be…”). But when it comes to humans, there is a different tone. Elohim says: “Let us make humankind in our own image”. And then it says: “So God created man in His own image, in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them” (Genesis 1:27).

Story Two says nothing about the man being made in God’s image, but it does have its own poignant way of expressing the elevated state of humanity. When Yahweh made the man, he formed him from the dust and then breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, and the man became a living person.

But there is a big difference between the two. In Story One, the image of God applies to “male and female”. In Story Two, it is only the man who receives the divine breath of life. The woman is fashioned out of the man’s body as a companion and helper. This is exactly the lesson the apostle Paul takes from this story in 1 Corinthians 11:7–9 where he says: “For a man should not have his head covered, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of man. For man does not originate from woman, but woman from man; for indeed man was not created for the woman’s sake, but woman for the man’s sake”. Notice how Paul rolls the stories into one, drawing the concept of God’s image from Story One and everything else from Story Two.

The biggest difference between the two stories is this: Story One shows us the goodness of creation (“and Elohim saw that it was good.”) There is no garden of Eden in Story One, no forbidden fruit⁶ nor any notion of the man and woman as childishly innocent (“naked and unashamed”). Every living thing has its place, whether in the sea or on land or in the air. The moon and stars mark out the portions of the year. The rising and setting sun marks out the days for labor and the day for rest. (These things became very important religious matters later in the Bible, which helps us locate in time the author of Story One). It is a good world, freshly made, unspoiled, full of life, and divinely ordered.

By contrast, Story Two begins (figuratively) with a loaded gun on the table, with the seeds of disaster already planted in the garden in the form of the forbidden tree of the knowledge of good and evil. “On the day that you eat from it, you will certainly die”, Yahweh tells the man immediately after creating him and putting him in the garden.

Story One has ended for now, but Story Two moves on to tell of a serpent in the garden who entices the woman to try some of that forbidden fruit. The details of that story are for another time, but let me mention the crushing consequences for the woman and the man, since they help us see the purpose of Story Two. Because of their disobedience, God declares that he will multiply the pain of childbirth for the woman, that her desire will be for her husband and her husband will rule over her. As for the man, God will curse the ground, and the man will have to work hard for his food until the day he returns to the dust. As for the serpent, he’ll be condemned to crawling around on the ground, eating dust. He’ll become a fearful and sneaky enemy to the man and the woman.

And these penalties aren’t just for this man, this woman, and this serpent. Their descendants will suffer the same fate. Which brings us to the purpose of the stories.

Story Two answers questions like: Why is life so hard? Why do people have to work so much just to survive? Why do women suffer and often die in childbirth? Why are there snakes that sometimes kill our livestock and our little ones? Why do men and women get married? Why is the man always the boss, not only at home, but everywhere? Why do we suffer and die?

In answer, Story Two says: “Well, God created the man first, breathed the breath of life right into the man’s nostrils. God made the woman later, and it was different. He made her out of the man’s rib, and he made her to be his helper. That’s her purpose. And life wasn’t always so hard. God gave them a beautiful garden to live in, and to cultivate. But the woman and the man couldn’t resist. They ate that fruit. So God punished them, punished us all. He cursed the earth and made childbearing difficult and dangerous. So our ancestors are to blame for the way things are. And truthfully, if we had been there, we probably would have done the same. So don’t think that God punishes the innocent. We’re all to blame. We deserve what we get.”

It’s the kind of story that, if you encountered it in a different book, you would understand that it wasn’t history, but rather a kind of story that you might tell around a campfire, one that is designed to give an imaginative explanation about why things are the way they are, and to defend the status quo. It’s also a story that can plant some profoundly damaging ideas in culture. And it has.

Story One thinks on a grander scale. While Story Two is about everyday life (marriage, hard work, suffering, and trying to make a living ), Story One is thinking about humanity’s place in creation. It says that God created a beautiful and orderly world, and every part of it has a place. Humankind is the pinnacle of life because humans are made in God’s image and given dominion over all living things. And yet, the story says, there is a God who is higher. He made everything, and in the process of doing that, he showed that the things other people worship as gods — heavenly bodies, rivers, trees — are subordinate to him. And, very importantly, God put his lights in the heavens to mark the times — times for holy festivals of religious observance and sacrifice, times to plant and harvest, days to work and a day each week on which no work may be done. This is God’s order, and it is good. You will do well to observe its boundaries.

I’ll say once more that if we encountered these stories in another place, we would quickly know that they were designed to (among other things) define boundaries, prescribe proper behavior, and control people. Which is exactly what the stories have been used for down through history, right up to the present moment. Anyone who advocates for gender equality, or for the right to divorce (or any right at all), or who questions gender norms, or champions a woman’s right to vote or to make decisions about her own body — can be (and have been) directed to these stories of why things are the way they are.

The Bible speaks with many voices from many perspectives, and not every text agrees with every other. This was not obvious to me in my ministry days because I was committed to an idea of the Bible that allowed it to speak with only one voice. How fascinating it is, then, to find such diversity in the first two chapters.

item.title: Does Morality Require God?
item.content:encoded:
Kath: “If you're an atheist, and you don't believe in an afterlife, if you don't believe in heaven and hell and all that, why don't you just go around raping and murdering as much as you want?”

Tony: “I do.”

Kath: “What?”

Tony: “I do go around raping and murdering as much as I want…which is not at all.”

That exchange is from an episode of Ricky Gervais' sad sweet comedy series Afterlife, and it provides a nice introduction to common ideas about God and morality — ideas like these:

“If you don't believe in God, you have no basis for morality.”

“Without God, right and wrong are only matters of preference. I prefer you don't murder me, but that doesn't make it wrong.”

“Without God, all things are permitted.”

The idea is that, without a higher authority to set the rules and penalize rule-breakers, there cannot be any objective standard for determining right and wrong.

I used to think that was a decent argument for God. Now it strikes me more as a useful argument for defending a religion and a religious text.

A common retort to this argument, from atheists: “If the only thing that keeps you from murdering people is that God will send you to hell for it, you aren't a moral person. You're just afraid of the consequences.”

That might be true, but it doesn't accurately describe what many Christians think. In a functioning and fairly safe society where there is enough food and at least a little hope that the average person can better their lot, few believers refrain from murder just because God says “Thou shalt not kill”. Instead, they “go around raping and murdering as much as (they) want…which is not at all.”

No, the idea that God is the basis of our morality (as I used to preach it) goes more like this:

Just as God laid down physical laws like gravity, he also established moral laws: You shall not steal, you shall not commit murder, you shall help your neighbors out when they need it. These ideas about right and wrong seem to be wired into humanity. After all, cultures all over the world have independently arrived at similar moral frameworks where theft and adultery and lying are condemned, and trustworthiness, courage, and loyalty are praised. Sure, there are differences of opinion as to what is the exact definition of murder (Can you kill in self-defense? In war? What about capital punishment?) And there are arguments about who the laws apply to (kings, chieftains and presidents can order quite a bit of killing). But the morals themselves are much the same from culture to culture. And the reason for this is that God, the Great Lawgiver, created a set of laws for us to live by and (in some undefined way) placed them in our hearts.

The paragraph above is the essence of what I thought and preached about morality during my ministry, and it was strongly informed by C.S. Lewis, who said that it is impossible to imagine a truly different kind of morality where, for example, cowards were considered heroes and people who murdered their families were admired. Lewis concluded that morality is not created tribe by tribe but rather is built into the universe, much like gravity, and we contend against it at our own peril. He also used this as an argument for belief in God.

So the argument that believers (at least informed believers) make isn't that people would be killing each other if they weren't afraid of God. It's that God has provided all people with a moral law that we cannot shake. You don't even need to know about God or read the Bible or see the 10 Commandments posted at school to know right from wrong (at a basic level).

That argument struck a chord with me when I was younger. It flips the question “If there is a God, why does he allow people to do so much evil?” by asking “Well if there is no God, why do people do anything good?”

But I later realized that there is a more natural way to explain our common morality, one that doesn't rely on an unseen God and an unproven method. Namely, some behaviors simply work better than others to produce human survival and flourishing.

Imagine ten prehistoric families who band together in a primitive and hostile world. They are more likely to survive and reproduce than one strong person going it alone. But those ten families can't survive if even a few people in the group are given to lying, stealing, treachery, cowardice, laziness, or even gluttony (when food is scarce). Such people would have to be left behind. And people who exhibit qualities that help the tribe (courage, honesty, industry) would be rewarded, and held up as examples.

People say that without God, morality is whatever you want it to be, but it really isn't. There are certain actions that help people work together and thrive. There are other actions that work against that goal.

Of course, people have always differed about who is required to obey the moral rules (and C. S. Lewis makes this point very well). That ten-family tribe can't tolerate theft or murder within the tribe. But in their dealings with outsiders, theft and murder are very likely the main order of business. It's a rough world and so it has to be us against them.

This of course is the story of human history — warring tribes killing each other in a fight for survival, yet practicing a very pragmatic morality with each other. Even Jesus noted this when he said that if you treat only your own people well, what are you doing more than the rest of humankind? Then he issued a call for a moral act that no one would call innate, and which is not often practiced by his followers: “Love your enemies.”

And now comes the big problem with the idea that God gives us a moral code: With God on our side, it seems that anything is permitted. One example: In the book of Numbers 31:14–18, after a battle with the Midianites in which the Israelite soldiers failed to slaughter all the non-combatants, Moses, the representative of God, had the following reaction:

But Moses was angry with the officers of the army, the commanders of thousands and the commanders of hundreds, who had come from service in the war. And Moses said to them, “Have you spared all the women? Behold, they caused the sons of Israel, through the counsel of Balaam, to be unfaithful to the Lord in the matter of Peor, so that the plague took place among the congregation of the Lord! Now therefore, kill every male among the little ones, and kill every woman who has known a man intimately. However, all the girls who have not known a man intimately, keep alive for yourselves.*

So, the moral guidance from God's prophet is this: 1) Kill all the boys (after all, they'll grow up to be our enemies); 2) Kill all the grown women, for they have been “spoiled” sexually, and they are temptresses who seduced our men and brought about a plague; 3) But as for the virgin girls? Consider them your reward.

For various reasons, I don't think this atrocious event really took place. I think it is a story to illustrate a point. But the point is that, with God, standards of right and wrong go out the window, and any atrocity is justified if someone with enough authority says that God commands it. Where is the innate, God-given moral code in that?

A few years ago, I asked a young man about this — a fine, moral, Christian guy who really is a decent and kind husband and father. He said that, yes, some atrocious things could be acceptable if God required them. I said that this could lead to some very dark places. He agreed, but stood firm in his conviction.

In my opinion, he is a good young man who nevertheless has been poisoned in his thinking by the very religion which gave his life direction at a time when he felt lost.

The great achievement of the Enlightenment with regard to morality is the expansion of the concept of “our tribe” to include more and more people — women, slaves, people of other races. Christians like to claim credit for most of these advances, but in truth Christians have rarely led the way in such matters. Instead, Christians in power have almost always curtailed freedoms, contracted the definition of the favored tribe, and used power to silence (or eliminate) contrary voices. This is what we see playing out before us in America today.

I'm not saying that there aren't some very good Christians. A few of the finest people I know are (or were) evangelical Christians. It is possible for Christianity to give direction and purpose to a directionless person and to put their life on a better path. But the same can be said for Islam or Alcoholics Anonymous or Crossfit, etc.

In my experience, though, Christians who are very good people either set aside some of the prejudices from the faith that limit their goodness, or else their own goodness is limited by the same.

So: “Without God, everything is permitted?” “Without God, there is nothing objective upon which to base morality?” I have come to think that it's just the opposite. If you believe that God is on your side, “everything is permitted for the sake of carrying out “God's will”.

But if you know that we're all in this life together, you'll see that morality isn't all that complicated and it doesn't require “divine hard-wiring” to explain it.
